speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER-TABLING OF REPORT ON DIVERSION OF WATER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from time to time there have been requests for the tabling of a report that was commissioned in 1955 on a possible diversion of water from the Columbia river to the Fraser river. As the report was related to the negotiations which had been undertaken with the United States relating to the Columbia river treaty, it was the policy of the previous government not to make the report public. The present government also felt that the report should not be released before negotiations by this government were completed relative to co-operative development of the Columbia river in Canada.
Now that these negotiations have reached successful completion with the signing of the agreements on January 22, 1964, I take this earliest opportunity to table one copy of the report which bears the title "Report on an investigation of Columbia to Fraser river diversion project, 1956", which was prepared by the B.C. Engineering Company Limited; also two copies of a paper which summarizes the findings contained in the report.
Shortly put, the report is not optimistic with regard to the cost at which power could be produced on the Thompson and lower Fraser rivers, either with or without a diversion from the Columbia. Without such a diversion the production cost is estimated at 9.7 mills per kilowatt hour for firm energy, and 6.75 mills for firm plus secondary energy. With the Columbia diversion the cost is estimated at 8 mills for firm energy and 6.95 mills for firm plus secondary. The increment of energy actually provided by the diversion is estimated to cost 7.1 mills per kilowatt hour when delivered to loads in Vancouver.
In arriving at this cost the report does not charge the diversion proposal for any portion of the cost of dams on the Columbia river required for the regulation and diversion of the water. The report does not go into the fishery problem, which is a major one, although it does deal with the cost of fish passages at the proposed dams.
As the report is very bulky, I regret that it is not possible to provide copies to individual members. However, they will be able to have access to it among the papers of the house.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to say something about this in view of the fact that the Department of National Defence was responsible. On Friday last the right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to what he termed "the deplorable armoury break-ins" and asked what security measures were being taken for the storage of weapons. In my answer I informed the house that as a result of the recommendation of the special commission which had been set up following

Inquiries of the Ministry the robbery of the armoury in Montreal, all small arms and ammunition were being withdrawn from reserve establishments where maximum security could not be provided. This was a temporary measure until it was possible to implement longer term measures. The services were informed that this order should include the province of Quebec and areas in the provinces of Ontario and New Brunswick adjacent to Quebec. The interpretation of the order has not been uniform, which has resulted in some obvious anomalies, such as the action taken at Windsor; but I should point out that the action taken by the armed forces was aimed at ensuring the security of all arms and ammunition in the minimum time possible.
I might add with regard to ammunition that some reserve units held large quantities, and it was decided some time ago that these should be withdrawn to central depots and only sufficient ammunition would be issued to meet immediate training needs.
Having asked on Friday what steps were being taken to secure weapons, yesterday the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, in a display of indignation, questioned the action taken with regard to the cadet unit at Ashbury College. He termed the activities of the members of the Canadian army as an invasion of privacy, repeatedly referred to the incident as a search, and even asked the Minister of Justice if a search warrant had been issued.
This is what actually happened. Following the order last Friday, headquarters central command of the Canadian army issued instructions for the withdrawal of weapons, the property of the Department of National Defence, from units including certain cadet corps in eastern Ontario areas. A party selected for the Ottawa area left Kingston, Ontario, at
7.30	on the evening of February 21 with instructions to collect the small arms from Ashbury College cadet corps and other cadet corps in the Ottawa area. The chief instructors of these cadet corps were informed and, in so far as Ashbury College was concerned, the estimated time of arrival was given as
9.30	p.m. However, due to the breakdown of the vehicle involved, there was an unavoidable delay.

subtopic: ROCKCLIFFE PARK, OTTAWA    REMOVAL OF ARMS FROM ASHBURY COLLEGE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ROCKCLIFFE PARK, OTTAWA    REMOVAL OF ARMS FROM ASHBURY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Some of the vehicles acquired by the government of the right hon. gentleman are not as reliable as they should be.
Again, the chief instructor of the cadet corps was informed. The party actually arrived at Ashbury College at 12.45 of the morning of February 22 and were met by the chief instructor, Captain Anderson, who gave his full co-operation to the army unit. The weapons and stores were removed from

two rooms in the basement as quickly as possible. These included ten FN rifles, thirty-seven .303 rifles, six .22 rifles, one hundred and fifty .22 Cooey rifles and four .303 Bren guns.
The action taken by the army was in complete conformity with the original order, and the only regrettable aspect was the late arrival of the party. I should emphasize, however, that at the time of the removal of the small arms no objection was made. On the contrary, the utmost co-operation was given by all concerned. I should point out also that the removal of small arms from other cadet corps units was carried out without any other incident being reported. In fact these cadet corps expressed full understanding of the reasons for withdrawal of weapons, and all assistant cadet instructors received complete co-operation. As I said yesterday, while the party from Kingston was armed, the ammunition was carried in pouches and bayonets were not in place, as was suggested by the right hon. gentleman opposite.
I am fully aware of the inconvenience to the members of the reserve and cadet units involved, who have generally shown complete understanding of the reasons for such action. May I repeat that these are temporary measures which have been taken until such time as the individual inspection of units can take place and proper safeguards are afforded. This individual inspection of units by senior officers has commenced. Following their report in each case that satisfactory arrangements are available, reinstatement of small arms will take place. This action will be implemented as expeditiously as possible, but it must be realized that in view of the large number of units involved some time will elapse before the task can be completed in full. I am sure that the temporary inconvenience caused reserve and cadet units, which I regret as much as anyone else, will be accepted in good grace as preferable to a further loss of weapons to unauthorized persons.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON U.S ACTION ON TAKE-OVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked the Minister of Justice some questions with respect to the acquisition of the John Labatt brewery by the Joseph Schlitz brewery of Milwaukee. I wonder if he is prepared to 20220-17J
Inquiries of the Ministry give me an answer now, and whether he could at the same time tell the house if the restrictive trade practices branch of his department could look into the whole matter with a view to seeing whether there is any violation of the anti-trust and anti-merger legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LABATT BREWING COMPANY
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON U.S ACTION ON TAKE-OVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for having waited until today to put the question again after having given me notice. I should like to answer the first question which was left unanswered on Hansard. He asked whether any representations were made to my department for intervention or action with respect to merger procedures, and the answer is no; no demands or requests were made to my department for that purpose.
In order to give the house an up to date report on the situation, and in answer to the general question, I shall read from a prepared answer which I have before me On February 18 the United States government notified the Canadian government of the proposed civil anti-trust proceedings in the United States against the merger of Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company of Milwaukee and John Labatt Limited of London, Ontario, and invited our comments. This was' in accordance with the understanding reached between our governments in 1959-that is between the former attorney general Mr! Fulton and Mr. Rogers, who was then the attorney general of the United States-to the effect that discussion will be held at the appropriate stage when it becomes apparent that interests in one of our countries are likely to be affected by the enforcement of the anti-trust laws of the other. The object is to avoid possible infringements of sovereignty such as might occur if the enforcement of the United States law had an effect in Canada that conflicted with Canadian anti-combines law or Canadian business or commercial policy, or affected the operation m Canada of a Canadian business.
Although an interim restraining order was made in the United States courts the following day, the United States government informed us that this step had to be taken promptly to preserve the status quo and that our comments in the matter would nevertheless be welcomed before the trial of the main issues, for which there would be adequate opportunity.
Having carefully studied the matter, I concluded that the situation does not appear to give rise to any conflict with Canadian anti-combines law and commercial policy, and that no action is contemplated in the United States courts that would affect the

Inquiries of the Ministry commercial operations of Labatt's in Canada. In my opinion this is a matter of concern to the domestic economy of the United States: the United States authorities are seeking to restrain a United States company from acquiring or retaining assets that will increase its power in the United States domestic market.
In all the circumstances my colleagues and I have formed the view, on the basis of our present information, that there is no occasion for the Canadian government to intervene, and a reply has gone to the United States government accordingly. For the information of the house a copy of the reply will be tabled. I might add that it is my intention to keep under review and to pursue further the question of any possible overlapping in the jurisdictional sense between the anticombines legislation of Canada and the United States anti-trust laws.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Jean-Pierre Cote (Longueuil) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne who fulfilled their task with spirit and great talent.
The state is a group of citizens who, because they belong to the same community, must submit to a common behaviour. To make that possible, those men chose the government which, in their opinion, seems to be in the best position, because of its nature, quality and composition, to meet their present needs as well as their hopes and aspirations.

That double duty of the government should not be misunderstood; the government must at the same time see to immediate necessities and develop plans in order to enable each and every citizen to accomplish, in the most favourable conditions, the things he considers as the most precious.
While we enjoy the benefits of democracy, we should not be complacent in our felicity. We will keep it only if we can discern the spirit which is under the surface, if we can remain fully aware of the great moral principles as well as of the material and external characteristics of this democracy which we profess to cherish and defend.
Is there too much idealism in this conception of government? A government must have ideals; otherwise it will not be equal to its task. We cannot exist without government. The best form of government, in our mind, according to our aspirations, is the government conducted by upright men, endowed with the necessary qualities to fulfil the obligations of a government.
In order to perform its mission as required, a government must have definite objectives, concrete goals. These objectives will vary from one country to another, with the circumstances and the environment, but the supreme criterion, the essential question will always remain the same: Confronted with actual problems and with prosperity, do the citizens enjoy the required protection and security?
This prompts us, particularly in Canada where ethnical, cultural and even economic problems are becoming more and more prominent, to ask ourselves serious questions. Integrity is one of the essential qualities of any government. A government draws its strength from the certainty, from the firm belief of the governed that the rulers do not hide anything and speak the truth.
Whenever a representative is elected by the people, he enters the government, not politics. A political party must strive to unite those who share the same ideas on certain questions, so as to enable them to put their principles into practice. After hearing the views expressed in the course of a debate, a member of parliament has the duty to arrive at an opinion of his own; he also must use his influence to act in accordance with the interests of the population as a whole.
Canada is divided into several areas- geographically, economically, historically- all of which often have conflicting interests. Representative government is the one where the member of the House of Commons should be ready to examine the claims from his electoral district in the light of Canada's interests, as a whole. The people as well as their representatives should think as Canadians, but they should also keep in mind that 20220-18
The Address-Mr. Matte all Canadians are equal. If this question of unity has been much discussed since the beginning of this session, it is due to its great importance.
The government holds its authority from the people; in turn, the people must know the mechanism of government in order to exercise their right for its functioning. A well informed public opinion will resist the trend which is, after all, only apathy and which consists in dissociating oneself from all political activity. Negligence in exercising one's rights often results in social scepticism and defeatism. However, to speak of indolence is often to conceal something else.
Fewer and fewer people vote in such and such a way because their parents did so, but there are still a great number whose vote is influenced by discussions on topics of the day. Those who have dealt with political matters in the last decade know where such an uncommitted vote can lead.
The prime and most obvious duty of any taxpayer is to elect representatives who commend themselves by their intelligence and their integrity. Every voter should require of the candidate seeking his support a statement on the policy he intends to advocate, something clear, unequivocal, definite, rather than vague and obscure statements. In my opinion, the present government is to be commended for its policy and its speech from the throne.
Canada is a federative state. The legal basis for this federation is an act of the imperial parliament known as the British North America Act of 1867 and the amendments thereto.
We propose to celebrate our centennial in three years. More and more, the question is raised: how will that be done? What importance will it have for the Canadian people? Are all Canadians attached to confederation? Are there some who would like to break away? How many? Why have they come to that conclusion? Are their reasons serious? Are those reasons irrevocable?
Would it be that such a situation is taking shape because Canada does not have the type of government it needs, because in view of our parliamentary system, all Canadians are not equal partners in the country and in every region? Would it be that our parliamentary institutions have become incapable of meeting those requirements? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker.
A government is judged on its achievements. Therefore, we must ask ourselves questions like these: what is its program? How is this program to be carried out? Does the government stick to its promises? We could add: does it repeat the same promises

The Address-Mr. Matte everywhere and to everyone? Does it advocate everywhere the same program? Does it propose to all Canadians the same steps to carry it out?
It is at least partly in the light of such questions that we must consider the recent attitudes of the French speaking Canadian citizens-particularly the French Canadians In Quebec as well as their complaints, and that is preci ely what I mean to do. Our Intentions are evidently honest, but is that honesty always followed by realistic and practical action? Our Canadian civilization is based on a social heritage of which many other countries could be envious. Our philosophy of life requires greatness from our leaders, honesty in our promises and faithfulness towards all our citizens.
A political crisis arises every time our institutions seem to stop like mechanical toys which have become unsprung. There are in fact times when we turn our backs to the lofty heights of individual freedom and responsibilities so dearly bought by our forefathers and retrograde in the dark valleys of bondage and servitude, and even bloody revolutions.
I am sure that most Canadians vote with the desire of choosing the best possible government. In choosing a government, a nation must look for superiority, free itself from prejudice, distinguish what makes the value of government and convince itself that mediocrity will never be a substitute for excellence.
Canada has chosen a Liberal government. The election of our party to the administration of the country is a rather recent event. All citizens have still fresh in their memory our campaign platform which led us to victory. And it is with that program that we want to administer and give Canada and all Canadians the prosperity, the security and the pride that should be every Canadian's lot. The policy that won us the electorate's confidence is also the policy with which the Liberal party began, right after the election, to administer the country. The first session and the present speech from the throne prove it.
The province of Quebec, a highly rural riding which I represent, strongly contributed to the Liberal victory. The province knew exactly what it could expect from each party. It is often said that the French Canadians in the province of Quebec resent confederation. It would seem that it is not confederation they resent, but the way it has often been applied.
Equal partners throughout the country, according to the spirit of confederation, they do not want to be considered as second-zone citizens in any part of the country. All sorts

of promises were made to them in the past. We have often seen our people disinterest themselves totally from the federal question. They had made too many requests; they had received too many promises which went unfulfilled. So, they decided not to expect anything any more from Ottawa. In a sense, they isolated themselves. They considered they were treated as foreigners, and they decided to stay at home.
For months there has been talk of bicul-turalism, of equal rights. These French Canadians have in Ottawa more ministers than ever. Our government became aware of their claims. The French Canadians have been awakened, as it were, to the federal institutions. But we must not be blind to the fact that this interest finds expression in two ways. There are some who proclaim the time has come for the province of Quebec to constitute itself into a separate state, to sever its links with the rest of the country, because it is too late to expect anything else. There are others-and they are the great majority- who say another chance, whole and honest, should be given confederation to show what it can do for the French speaking Canadians living in Canada, not only in Quebec, where French Canadians are the majority, but in all the other provinces, where they consider themselves as equal citizens in every respect.
I say, I declare and I repeat every day to my French speaking fellow citizens: It is more than ever essential that French Canadians be interested in federal affairs, not only to demand the respect of their language, a distinctive flag and national anthem, but also a more active participation in the economy of the country. They wish, of course, in these days of great strides to take in hand the promotion of the rights and privileges which they consider as their own in every sphere of federal activity. They must have full and complete confidence in the program set forth by the Liberal party at election time and which is exactly the same as the one which the government intends to implement.
We must strengthen national unity by placing on the same footing the two founding races in this country, while taking into account the contribution of other races to our national culture:
Thus spoke our great Prime Minister at the national meeting of the national federation of the Liberal party held in Ottawa on February 11, 1963.
He added:
As far as national unity is concerned, and especially the acceptance of the one principle on which that unity can be based I wish to state that it can only be based on the principle of equality of the two races which established confederation.
Canada is a bicultural and bilingual country, and it is impossible to ensure the survival of confederation or even to celebrate its centennial in

worthy fashion if we ignore that principle. We have to remember that French Canadians do not constitute a minority which enjoys special rights in but one province. They have rights equal to those of English Canadians and they share the benefits and responsibilities of our national development. That is why the Liberal government was duty-bound to set up a royal commission which was to consult the various provincial governments in order to find out how that principle can be applied. If we attain that objective-and it would be a marvellous achievement to mark the centennial celebrations-Canada will keep on progressing as a true federation. We wish to ensure national unity according to that principle.
Since he was put in office, the Prime Minister has not been talking differently and all his actions up to now indicate how much he believes in biculturalism.
I should now like to pay him a tribute for the splendid speech he made in the house last week; he showed once more his greatness and his broadmindedness. He is duly recognized as one of the greatest, if not the greatest, of all the Canadian prime ministers.
The former member for Laurier, now high commissioner in England-to whom I offer my congratulations and very best wishes of success-talking about the problem of biculturalism, quite rightly recalled that the present Prime Minister had been the first Anglo-Saxon leader to commit himself to the setting up of an inquiry intended to make French Canadians equal partners within the nation.
The day is gone, he said, when the French Canadians, dissatisfied with not being heard, simply gave up any attempt to raise their voices.
They do not claim special privileges, they want recognition, in practice, of the fact that they are everywhere equal partners in a confederation which they helped to found (and which was an essential requirement then). They want for their compatriots in the other provinces a treatment similar to that enjoyed by the English speaking Canadians living in Quebec. Should that request be disregarded, then the uneasiness and even the bitterness of the French Canadians would be directed against confederation and separatism would really spread.
That is not to be wished for either group, but rather understanding in action on both sides.
As I said before, the former minister of justice speaks in the most realistic way when he says:
If we intend to celebrate the centennial only by building monuments and organizing festivals and exhibitions a bitter awakening is in store for us, because the unity we will celebrate then, if it still exists, will surely be just an imitation of the real thing.
If we wish to celebrate the centennial of confederation together, we must get our minds together as we have done in the past and think not only about what we are but about what we want to become. We can no longer be satisfied with respecting each other in our mutual isolation. We 20220-18i
The Address-Mr. Matte
must take this opportunity which may be our last chance, to reaffirm collectively our will to live together on a truly equal footing.
Mr. Chevrier has repeated those remarks time and again. From his experience, they expressed a deep conviction and contained a program which he has always fought for passionately.
I should also like to say that I have truly marvelled at the harmony and understanding which prevails among all Liberal members in the house.
They exchange ideas in brotherly fashion.
I would have liked to deal with the importance and advisability of extending the Three Rivers harbour, which I am asking for in the Champlain riding. I shall refer to this matter later on.
Even though part of my constituency has not been considered as a designated area, because it failed to meet required standards, the unemployment problem is of great concern to us.
Mr. Speaker, in the past, the province of Quebec was essentially an agricultural province. It has become industrialized a great deal since, but farming remains an important industry in Quebec. Eastern farmers have known and still experience difficult years. They were under the impression that the Department of Agriculture existed solely for the other part of Canada. They considered themselves as foreigners in Ottawa.
Westerners are wheat growers and we wish them prosperity; easterners are mainly engaged in the dairy industry. While they were planning their program, the Liberals knew that the Quebec farmers as well as those from Ontario and the maritimes, needed a minister specifically to take care of their problems which greatly differ. That is why the speech from the throne mentions that a measure will be presented to provide for a minister responsible for rural development. This will be a new department created by the government during this session. We do not harbour any grievances towards the western farmers on account of their prosperity; we wish them well-besides, they also have their problems. I have been very fortunate in touring a part of their territory last year and I hope that all the members will have the opportunity of visiting all parts of Canada; it would enable us to understand one another better and to understand each other's problems.
We also would like our problems to get some consideration, so that we should also experience prosperity, thanks to the dairy industry, which is the very basis of farm economy and ensures our farmers the greater part of their income.
We should take the necessary measures to control the farming industry to a higher

The Address-Mr. Ricard degree by means of a stronger "advisory control" based on statistics, while keeping in mind that stability of prices more particularly for feed grain, is essential if we want to succeed.
Following the great evolution in Quebec, there is a growing awareness that some aspect has been neglected there. People are anxious to believe in confederation.
Mr. Speaker, it is not with animosity, but with trust that one obtains a federal government which strives for national unity and knows the right means for making Canadians everywhere in this country equal partners in the magnificent endeavour to make Canada a great and prosperous country in which there will be recognition, understanding and mutual respect for every uniting and common factor, as well as for existing diversity. That is what the Liberal party promised Canadians. It has already started applying the measures which will at last answer all the aspirations of all right-minded people in my county of Champlain, in my province and my country.
If we understand each other, if we love each other really in our diversity, we shall be able to celebrate the centenary of this confederation with enthusiasm for the benefit of this country and all its citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like previous speakers, I wish to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have made a superhuman effort to do their job and they deserve that we say it out loud. In view of the emptiness of the speech from the throne, it is easy to see that they had to devote several hours to the preparation of their speeches and the fact that they performed their task in such an elegant fashion is all to their credit.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss matters concerning my constituency, but since I wish to leave enough time to the following speakers and I also wish to move an amendment, I will only make a few remarks, reserving the right to bring up these matters later on.
For instance, as far as the interests of my riding are concerned, I shall take a few minutes of the time of the house on some future occasion to deal with the matter of the St. Pie penitentiary so as to show with what contempt and in what offhand manner the former minister of justice (Mr. Chevrier) has been grossly unfair toward my constituency. This is enough for now, but I shall bring up the subject later on.
As I said earlier, the speech from the throne, which will surely go down in history

on account of its emptiness, is useless because it provides absolutely nothing either for the workers or for the farmers. In view of the fact that I have the honour to represent in this house an electoral district made up of these two classes of the society, practically in equal parts, I shall take only a few minutes to make some remarks on the needs of my constituents.
Mr. Speaker, if you exclude from this speech from the throne, the continuation of the measures instituted by the Conservative government, you will conclude that it contains nothing new.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that during the election campaign of 1962, as well as that of 1963, those who are now sitting on the treasury benches and are members of this cabinet were pretending to know all the answers to our questions; they were going to solve in no time at all, all those alarming problems facing farmers and workers alike.
You will especially recall, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian farmers have been presented as the great architects of the present-day community, and it was even said that we had all the necessary ability to give happiness and satisfaction, in short an earthly paradise, to the majority of those people who deserve so much on account of their endeavours to provide food for the nation.
There may be nothing for farmers in the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, but there is nothing for workers either.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that during the sessions prior to the last general election of 1963, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) in particular used to be very sorry for the unemployed. He said at the time that he had in his files the legislation that should be passed to stop unemployment in a jiffy.
We just have to compare the situation today with that prevailing at that time to find that there are now 466,000 people without jobs throughout Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Much fewer than before.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And those men, Mr. Speaker, were to suppress unemployment entirely. Well, I shall tell those who are sitting on the treasury benches, as well as those who are making interjections from their seats in the back: You have now a free hand, you can go ahead, so please carry out the program you prepared during the election and, do something at last, because, during the nine months you have been at the helm in Canada, you have, as yet, done nothing worth while.

It is high time to tackle this task, as you promised to Canadian people, and which is expected from you. Put an end to the inertia which has taken hold of you since April 1963; get going and arouse yourselves from your torpor and do something, because the Canadian people are anxious to see you make a start.
We were told, Mr. Speaker, you will recall, that 60 days would suffice a Liberal government to accomplish much more than the Conservative party did during the years it presided over the fortunes of the country.
Indeed, several decisions were taken, but there were also, it must be admitted, indecision and do-nothing periods during those 60 days which marked the beginning of the Liberal government. Our friends opposite have no doubt accomplished something.
First of all, they accepted nuclear arms, even without consulting parliament. They established an 11 per cent tax on construction materials, which tremendously contributed to a rise in the cost of living, which, by the way, is presently the highest in the whole history of Canada. They have greatly tarnished Canada's reputation abroad by imposing a 30 per cent tax on securities, a tax which they withdrew later on under the pressure exerted by financiers, their friends. They also reduced farmers' income by removing the premium of 25 cents per hundred pounds of milk sold to manufacturers.
A short while ago I was listening to my good friend from Champlain (Mr. Matte), who said a better chance, more advantages, should be granted to dairy farmers. Assuredly, and the present government gave many advantages to farmers-it reduced their income.
What have they done besides that, Mr. Speaker? Well, they showed their contempt for the autonomy of the provinces when they tried to enter certain fields reserved to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I am not the only one to say so, since Mr. Levesque, Mr. Lesage and Mr. Gerin-Lajoie stated that the present Liberal government was trying to infiltrate into fields specially reserved to the provinces, and in particular the province of Quebec.
Have they done a great deal for the Gaspe area? The government of which I was a member decided to build a railroad between Ma-tane and St. Anne des Monts to assist the economic development of the area. What help did the Liberal government give that area? When it came to power it quickly cancelled that railroad project and since then the people of the Gaspe peninsula and the member for Gaspe have been deploring that action.

The Address-Mr. Ricard

speechtext:
Did you finish your own speech?
Mr. Speaker, the remarks of my hon. friend from Gaspe will not disturb me. I simply ask him whether he would deny that the railroad project was decided by the Conservative government and was then cancelled by the Liberal government as soon as it assumed office.
Now, let us go on, Mr. Speaker. Let us see what the present Liberal government did to raise the standard of living. It collected from the Canadian taxpayers new taxes in the post office. You know that the rates changed drastically. Some rates, for instance, were increased by 50 per cent and if I had the time I would give you the list of the various increases, but I will simply say that these postal rate increases will be paid by the entire Canadian population which certainly expected something else after all the promises made by the Liberal party in the election campaign.
May I mention also the tax increase from 3 to 4 per cent and this, in order to provide for a pension fund. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that during the election that tax was levied on salaries. It was simply said that once in office the Liberal party would set up a pension fund for everybody and that all Canadians would benefit from it immediately. But if we compare their words with the action taken, we find what we are discussing now, that is a tremendous difference between the promises and the action of the Liberals.
Under the Conservatives there was no tax on building materials or production machinery, but the financial wizard in Canada decided to impose an 11 per cent tax. Then he had to spread it out in instalments, because of the representations coming from all sides. He even spread it out later so it would be advantageous to all those who could take advantage of honest people.
He also disclosed a long time in advance the measures that the budget speech would contain concerning the levying and the withdrawal of certain taxes. During all that time we made all the representations we could to help the people because we know them well and we are their friends. We did all that was in our power to have that tax withdrawn. But no, the financial genius wants it that way and that 11 per cent tax will remain.

The Address-Mr. Ricard
I said a while ago that we had 466,000 unemployed in Canada. I discussed that matter a while ago and I shall not come back to it, but I must point out to you, Mr. Speaker, the huge difference between the attitude taken by the Liberals when in opposition and the one they take today now that they are in office.
If my memory serves me right, I think it was in November 1962 that the question of the president of the C.N.R., Mr. Gordon, came up in the house. Representations agreeable to my Liberal friends were made on several points. In the house they demanded that Mr. Gordon be fired immediately because, they said, he had shown contempt for French Canadians. What did they do as soon as they were in a position to act in that respect? They gave Mr. Gordon an extension. That shows how sincere they are; that is how they translate their words into action.
There is more than that however and I should like to take a few minutes to discuss matters which are of special concern to farmers.
Where are the defenders of our farmers? When they were sitting on this side of the house, the Liberals claimed to be the true representatives of farmers.
I have here a copy of the Liberal platform for the 1962 and 1963 elections. If you read that platform, you will see that our opponents, who called themselves the "seventy five", were astute indeed.
In the farm bulletin for May 1962, they published the program they would undertake to carry out as soon as they would come to power. What is the Minister of Agriculture waiting for to implement that program?
And they said they had all the answers.
One plank of the Liberal platform was the following:
Organization of marketing on a national basis.
Is there any mention of that in the speech from the throne?
Here is another plank:
Improved long term financing of co-operatives.
I see no indication in the speech from the throne of legislation to carry out that promise.
Here is another plank of the Liberal platform:
Realistic and systematic forecasting of the demand for grain and cattle.
Where are the measures likely to achieve this purpose?
I shall not go on, Mr. Speaker, because there is no end to unfulfilled Liberal promises.
And yet, you Liberals, more especially those from the province of Quebec, remember how much you speculated and gambled during the last election campaign on the necessity of appointing a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. It seems that you


have completely forgotten your promises. As a matter of fact, where is the minister of agriculture for eastern Canada whom you were crying for so vehemently when we were in office? You promised that this minister would be appointed as soon as you came into power. You are in a position to do so now, and yet, you do nothing; you even fail to keep your election promises.
Mr. Speaker, that is hardly surprising because apparently government members believe that the end justifies the means.
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this debate, it has been noted that the attitude of government members is completely different from what it was during the last sessions.
In fact, Liberal members from rural constituencies were showering the then minister of agriculture with all kinds of requests, maintaining that the Conservative party had failed to submit any project or to consider any measure to help farmers. However, what have they done since they are in power? They merely continue to follow the policy and implement the measures applied by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), who, according to experts and farming authorities, was the greatest minister of agriculture we ever had in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it would appear that our friends opposite have been told to talk about national unity, bilingualism and biculturalism so that their promises can be forgotten. I am wondering whether this is not the voice of their conscience forcing them to repair the harm they have done to Canadian unity in the past. I think they have a heavy load on their conscience, and this would explain why today, to live down all the harm they have caused, they feel compelled to take up the time of the house to talk of national unity and bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, I do not trust the word of those people and, judging by their past behaviour, I do not think the team now to be found on the cabinet benches has the qualifications needed, and I would even go so far as to say the sincerity, to promote national unity.
Is there a member who has been more vilified, more ridiculed and more slandered that the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker)?
During the election campaigns, more particularly in Quebec, they visited religious orders; they came to the most informal meetings to tarnish the reputation of the man who was prime minister for six years and to spread the most contemptible rumours about him.
They went everywhere in the province of Quebec and said to male and female members of religious orders: Do not vote for him,

he is a 32nd degree Mason. But did they have the courage to repeat the same thing in Ontario? No.
To those who would be inclined to believe that I indulge in exaggeration, I must say that I have some documents they will be able to check, which indicate that the Liberal party policy was to divide to better rule.
I have here an article written by Mr. Yves Michaud, which appeared in the St. Hyacinthe Le Clairon, showing clearly how racial feelings were being taken advantage of. Here it is:
In our opinion, the problem for French Canadians is not very complicated. On the one hand, you have Mr. Louis St. Laurent, leader of the Liberal party, who inspires Canadian policy at home and abroad and who knows how to give real meaning to Canadian unity. On the other hand, you have Mr. John Diefenbaker, leader of the Progressive Conservative party, who has shown, on many occasions, his resentment towards the French Canadian minority in our country.
Is that not playing on the heart strings and trying to stir up ill feeling between the races? And the same thing was tried against me. In my own riding, during the night of June 8 to June 9, 1957, a circular was distributed which said:
A vote for Ricard is a vote for Diefenbaker, and a vote for Diefenbaker is a vote for religious persecution.
And to think that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) defended in his own province of Saskatchewan, in 1922, teachers who taught French in the schools of that province.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals thought that there was something to be gained by distributing such propaganda; as a matter of fact, I am sure they made political capital out of that in some places.
Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard it said that the statements made in the province of Quebec by members on this side of the house are not the same as those they make in Toronto?
Yet, I have here an article according to which the Minister without Portfolio is alleged to have said that one must not say the same thing in Montreal as in Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, I used to be a school trustee in my home town and, as such, I know something of the problems with which the father of school children is faced. That is why it is a pleasure and an honour for me to move the following amendment.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth that the following words be added to the address in reply to the speech from the throne:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose the extension of family allowances to children 16 to 18 years of age who still attend school.
The Address-Mr. Chapdelaine
To conclude I should like to associate myself with the words that the Conservative leader for the province of Quebec, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), said here as reported on page 4155 of Hansard for October 29, 1963:
I am here to lend a hand to all members, be they French speaking or English speaking, who want to work for the good of our country. Indeed, such are the basic principles of the Conservative party which led to the birth of confederation as we know it today.
I would express only one wish, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative party, which gave confederation to Canada, be in power in 1967, in order that, all together, we may celebrate its centennial.
The Conservative party-and I am proud of it-since confederation has given the country ten prime ministers, who all ranked among the most brilliant in our country's history.

speechtext:
join the previous speakers to offer congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to congratulate the newly-elected members for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc and St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), and I shell express the wish their presence in this house be an asset for the province cf Quebec, which they represent, and for the whole of Canada.
In the past, I had the opportunity of putting forward my views on a necessary reform of parliamentary procedure and it would be useless to repeat my former suggestions, since they already appear in the record. Fortunately, since then, a committee to reform parliamentary procedure was established and the speech from the throne shows that the government intends to continue the work already begun by this committee.
However, I should like to call once again the attention of the house to a particular aspect of the changes which are to be made not only to the procedure of the house, but also to the ceremonies that take place at the opening of parliament. Again this year, we attended imposing ceremonies that seem useless to me, and to express my views on the subject, I could find no better words than the comments of Mr. Andre Laurendeau in Le Devoir, which show how antiquated and anachronistic those demonstrations are. This is what he had to say:
The strange ceremony by which parliament opens its sessions was broadcast on the C.B.C. Tuesday.
In a liturgy, usually, gestures are the symbol of actual facts. But this ceremony is more of a historical reconstitution. We are playing at the parliamentarian monarchy of the last century.
Who is running the affairs of Canada. The government and the members of the house: being plain,

The Address-Mr. Chapdelaine ordinary people, they are those we hardly see while the speech from the throne is being read. Yet, it is the government supported by a majority of house members, which dictated the words spoken by the Governor General.
Thus do appearances betray reality. Those who count have to be satisfied with the last places available, while those who no longer count have a monopoly on uniforms and all the trappings.
Those are considerations, Mr. Speaker, which I hope shall be seriously examined by the committee on parliamentary procedure. Without wishing to hurt anybody's feelings, I respectfully submit that we are no longer living in a century where we have to impress people with all sorts of trimmings and eyewash to make them believe we are playing an important role in this house.
A classic author said:
When not gifted with beauty, we must make up our face.
It would be much better to get to work with humility at the sober opening of the session to prove to the people later on that our work is worth while.
But since, this year again, we have to follow the established rule and talk for eight days, often to say nothing, I shall keep on talking a little more so as not to leave my place to someone else who probably thinks, the same as I do, that these discussions are as useless as they are empty. In a house with four parties and one group, I think it would be better to put the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the hands of a few members who could easily, in two days, wrap up what we take eight days to say. Especially, Mr. Speaker, in this case where we have to talk, not about the substance of the speech of the throne, but mainly about what it lacks. Once more, I should like to quote a comment by Mr. Laurendeau concerning the general outline of the policy of the Liberal party, as stated in the speech from the throne:
My government will attempt to make its full contribution to the maintenance of peace and the improvement of international relations; to the strengthening of our national unity through a cooperative federalism; to fostering the full employment of our people and the efficient growth of our economy; and to broadening the opportunities for a good life which should be open to all Canadians.
The slashing comment is as follows:
So that all parties might answer amen. And then the real debates begin.
Yet, it would be important to know what the present government intends to do, or when it intends to do something, if anything, about recognizing red China. But, last February 19 when I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) if his government was now contemplating, whatever the attitude of the United States, the possibility of recognizing red China, he answered,

without turning a hair, that Canada is a sovereign country and that its government would reach its own decision, taking into account only what concerns Canada and what comes within its jurisdiction.
That was an answer like the ones the minister usually gives, that is no answer at all, since everybody knows now that only the influence of the United States can prevent Canada from recognizing red China.
All Canadian politicians and all diplomats admit that it is no longer possible to ignore 600 million Chinese who have, on the international scene, an ever increasing influence. To refuse the dialogue with such a power is a diplomatic nonsense that cannot be justified by any reason in the circumstances; and the recent action taken by France should set an example to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who might take tangible action to prove to the rest of the world that Canada is a sovereign country.
Concerning a matter of less scope on the international scene but of some importance in Canada itself, I would like to say a few words on the problem of patronage which still exists in government, and which was inherited from the former administration, which in turn had inherited it from the previous one.
Everyone is familiar with the miniature scandal which arose when a Conservative member published a list of "consultants" which was in the possession of the former postmaster general. This scandal took a comical turn when the postmaster general, in order to justify himself, found no better way than to publish the "consultants" list which existed under the Conservative administration.
I should like at this time to address myself to the Minister of Justice, whose honesty, integrity and sincerity are unquestionable, and call to his attention a fact he ignores, I hope, and which he will be able to redress after I have told him about it.
A shameful patronage is now going on in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, under which in every city or area, public notaries are designated who will be the only ones entitled to prepare mortgage contracts for C.M.H.C. loans. In Sherbrooke, under the Conservative administration, four public notaries had been designated by the minister of justice, and they were immediately replaced by three notaries of Liberal allegiance after the April 8, 1963 election.
I understand that there may be some advantages in proceeding this way in some cases, but it is unthinkable that a young notary, at the beginning of his career, should be deprived of vital income when experienced notaries, with a good practice, who have

served in the ranks of the party in power, benefit by an additional source of income amounting to several thousand dollars when they could easily do without it and while young notaries are literally starving during their first years of practice.
If the Minister of Justice does not have the list of notaries who hold the rose bowl at this time as far as contracts with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are concerned, I can give it to him; at the same time, I could send him the list of all the other notaries in the area who are in dire need of work.
Since separatism, bilingualism, bicultural-ism and binationalism are current topics of conversation these days, I would be remiss if 1 did not make a few remarks about those questions. I should like to say first of all that I am not a separatist and that I openly condemn all extremists, no matter what side of the fence they stand on, because in his way, each of them works against the solution of a problem that neither French Canadians nor English Canadians can ignore.
May I commend the government for the efforts it is making in connection with this disagreement which is gathering momentum. I have great sympathy for the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who finds himself between two stools more often than he should but who still has found it possible, since he took office, to take steps which may not be satisfactory to everybody but which have none the less raised the discussion to the level of a dialogue.
I am thinking of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission which is travelling across the country at present to collect useful information. Even though some men in public life are questioning the merits of such a commission, I am convinced that individuals as intelligent and sincere as Messrs. Lauren-deau and Dunton would not have accepted this task if there had been no hope. You will tell me that hope is a plant that grows even in graveyards, but I say that where there is hope, there is life.
There is also the matter of federal-provincial conferences which have started and will continue to take place. During those conferences, a solution is sought by means of sound discussions, which is the normal way of doing things in civilized society. I prefer such an attitude to that of people who seek to thrust their views on others instead of having them discussed for fear they would be untenable. Such an attitude is typical of the weak.
I also prefer such a way of tackling problems, since an agreement has to be reached, to the attitude of those who are looking for extraordinary solutions copied from
The Address-Mr. Chapdelaine countries where the mentality and living conditions are as foreign to Canada as a rider to a cow.
Let us attempt to understand and enforce a document conceived by Canadians of both original racial groups for the Canadian people, a document entitled the British North America Act. Useless to add that it would be advisable to renovate it, to refurbish it, to bring it up to date, without bungling it or what would be worse, destroying the country which is the envy of all other nations. It is time to read over that agreement entered into between free men in 1867 and to meet our commitments on both sides.
If Quebec gets the tax share it is entitled to, if its rights in education are respected, I am convinced that most extremists will get closer to the centre, because some will get what they are entitled to and the others will not feel that they have given up what they believed was rightfully theirs.
I would like to add to that a truly bilingual capital, which would put an end to this dialogue between deaf people which even the least patriotic of French Canadians find frustrating when they come to their national capital, Ottawa.
We have no intention of asking that bilingualism be enforced throughout Canada. In some parts of the country, it would be just as ridiculous as trying to impose Chinese to the Russians. As soon as things come to light, English Canada is in a position to realize that we have been ignored in the federal civil service, especially at the higher levels. We simply want to enjoy equality as a nation and to be able to occupy positions in proportion to our population-strength and capacity being equal.
As all or practically all French speaking members can speak English, it would be appreciated throughout Canada if English speaking members would try to do the same with regard to French. This is a matter of courtesy and not an obligation or claim on our part.
In the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, there is also a mention of interest free loans to students. I do not want to deal with the constitutional aspects of these loans at this time, but I would just ask the government why it cannot think of granting interest free loans to municipalities, or for the building of public utility facilities? It would be possible, while safeguarding provincial autonomy, to make available to the various provincial and municipal organizations loans without interest, which would cut in half the cost of those public utility facilities, and would, consequently, decrease the burden of the taxpayers who have to pay twice the value of those facilities.

The Address-Mr. Chapdelaine
Again, we will be told that money does not grow on trees or fall from the sky like manna; and I shall answer that, like everybody, we are not stupid enough to think so. But, when we explain to the government or to economists that nothing would prevent amending the Bank Act so that the authority -to loan up to 12 times as much money as they have on deposit with the Bank of Canada -given those institutions by that legislation be gradually taken from these private enterprises which the chartered banks are, and transferred to the government, which would then be able to create its own money or credit that could be extended without interest, or with a simple carrying charge, to the provinces and municipalities. There has never been a single economist or banker who denied that such action was possible. Prove to us that it is impossible, and we shall cease to make impossible suggestions.
Existing governments, all over the world, whose economy is based on capitalism, somewhat fear state socialism or plain communism. It is because of that saving fear that they pass, reluctantly, socializing measures as needed at election time in order to gain the favour of the electorate; we are sinking more and more deeply into socialism for lack of a better solution. Therefore, it is the present state of capitalism which breeds socialism, and rather than correcting the deficiencies in capitalism, we fall stupidly into the arms of a monster which provides us day after day with renewed evidence of its inefficiency. Are wheat sales to red China and Russia not the tangible proof of the failure of state farms while, in western Canada, where even weeds would hardly grow at the beginning of our century, private enterprise and initiative have succeeded in growing gold.
To accept the socialist philosophy, we must accept as a premise that everything in capitalism is essentially bad and only then could we understand a government reluctantly accepting socialism since there is no other solution.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is the Social Credit solution which intends to correct the deficiencies of capitalism and, sooner or later, if governments do not take it into consideration, they will have to submit to pure and simple socialization.
Fortunately, the United States realized lately that they had to cut taxes in order to increase buying power, and I hope this government will also understand that and take similar steps in the near future.
Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some comments on the amendment moved by the Conservative party proposing to increase family allowances in the case of children from 16 to 18 years of age who still attend school.
[Mr. Chapdelaine.l
We are in complete agreement with such a measure, but we have confidence that the Liberal party, having advocated the same policy in its platform, will stand by its promises, and we think that, under the circumstances, that Progressive Conservative amendment is useless and just a scheme, since only yesterday the Conservative party voted against a similar amendment moved by the Ralliement Creditistes. Therefore, we do not attach to it more importance than it deserves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by associating myself with the tributes which have been paid to the mover and seconder of the address in reply, the hon. member for Longueuil and the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard. I should like also to associate myself with the compliments and good wishes which have been extended to those of my colleagues who have been newly called to the ministry.
The speech from the throne contains two items of special interest to my constituency. I refer to those parts which deal with the 12 mile limit and the fishery development program. We must wait until the legislation has been brought down before we can judge just how beneficial it will be, but since 80 per cent or more of my constituents are fishermen I should like to advise the government now that if the fishery development program is to be of any immediate benefit to the people of my riding it must contain at least four measures.
The first of these should provide for some means of easy credit whereby fishermen can obtain small loans for boats and gear without having to make any down payments. When it is considered that the average income of these fishermen is less than $1,000 a year, hon. members will understand that it is not possible for them to find funds for down payments, however small may be the sums required.
The second reauirement is an improvement in the bait service. At the present time we have two bait services in my province. One is supplied by the federal government and the other is supplied by private enterprise, mainly by the operators of fish processing plants. The difficulty is that when a fisherman gets his bait from a fish plant he is compelled to sell his fish to that plant, and is therefore not free to take advantage of any other market which may be available. He cannot choose a market where he might get a higher price. This is a situation which should be corrected.
The third requirement is an extension of the existing insurance coverage for boats and fishing gear. The fourth is some method of

compensation tor the lack of competition so as to ensure that fishermen receive the highest possible price for their catch.
The speech from the throne also indicates that steps are to be taken to expand markets for Canadian exports through the liberalization of world trade. Canada, with a domestic market of 19 million people and an industrial capacity sufficient for 50 million people, must sell her surplus products in foreign markets. To provide jobs for those who are presently unemployed as well as for the ever growing work force we must, therefore, continue to expand our world trade. This urgent necessity, together with the changing pattern of world trade, underlines the vital necessity of a new trading plan for Canada, a plan based on the new thinking which is being directed toward trade problems and trade development. Essentially, this new approach must be global in character; global trading with mass storage, mass distribution, continuous supply, cheap transportation and low distribution costs. Such a plan envisages the utilization of a global chain of entrepots or mass storage and distribution depots such as already exist in Hong Kong, Singapore, Beirut, Europort in Rotterdam and Colon in Panama.
In order to expand her world trade, Canada must have a link in this chain; in other words a Canadian equivalent of Europort, a Canadian entrepot, a showplace for Canada, a kind of giant supermarket where our products can be stored in readiness for mass distribution to the whole world, and where other nations can store their goods for mass distribution to North and South America. Viewed from this angle, a Canadian link in this world chain of entrepots becomes a necessity, and the logical location for it is on the south coast of Newfoundland. For more than 50 years people have dreamed of such an entrepot at Mortier bay in my riding of Burin-Burgeo, which is admirably located at a point where world trade routes and world shipping lanes converge. The time has now come when this dream can be translated into reality, and I urge the government to give careful consideration to this proposal and to do everything possible to bring it about. As a corollary to a trading plan for Canada we should also initiate a program to build a new Canadian merchant fleet so that our goods can be carried to world markets in Canadian ships.
The speech from the throne also makes reference to some measures to improve the efficiency of parliament. Last session great concern was expressed on both sides of this house and by members of all parties about the image of parliament which we were creating in the public mind. It is heartening to see again, at the beginning of this session, that similar convictions are being expressed.
The Address-Mr. Carter Some suggestions have been made as to procedures that may be adopted to compel us to make better use of parliamentary time, particularly as it applies to the question period.
Personally, in my opinion all that is necessary is to obey the rules we now have. For example, if we asked questions only of national importance and which required an urgent reply, our question period would seldom exceed 30 minutes. The same applies to points of order and to questions of privilege; if we would refrain from raising false points of order and false questions of privilege we would use up very little time in this way, and what time was devoted to this would be well spent. There should be no finger pointing about this, because no party and no member has any right to point the finger in this respect; we are all equally guilty of transgressing the house rules.
At the same time, the suggestions which have been put forward appear to me to be second best. They suggest an admission on our part that we do not intend to obey the rules, and that therefore instead of obeying the rules we will resort to devices to save parliament from the consequences of our reluctance to do what is right. In my opinion that is not a sign of maturity. We all have a duty and a responsibility to make parliament work, and it is better to obey the rules we have than to add to the rules and disregard them.
By making parliament work we would also take a long stride toward making confederation work. In a country like Canada there is bound to be a conflict of interest between one region and another. In a country with our historic background it is inevitable that problems of human relationships will arise between one group and another, between one race and another. These will require adjustments of attitudes and reconciliation of viewpoints.
However, there should be no problems between reasonable people which cannot be reconciled on a basis of what is right for the country as a whole, and personally I see no need to tear our country apart in the process. If we make confederation work we shall set a good example in making democracy work; and we should never forget that democracy is still on trial and fighting for its life. The free world is still engaged in a life and death conflict with world communism. Improved economic conditions and overpreoccupation with our own problems tend to make us forget that fact. But the communists have not abandoned their unswerving commitment to our destruction; they still intend to bury us, and any disagreement between them is only over the best way to do it.

The Address-Mr. Carter
Our problem of national unity is not unrelated to this great world problem. Any division that weakens Canada also weakens the free world and democracy everywhere, and at the same time we give comfort and aid to our enemies. Parties with different goals and viewpoints should reflect whether it is worth while to gain their own particular aims or their own particular aspirations if the end result is that we are going to wind up as slaves, as has happened to one third of the human race.
In the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, many speakers have dealt with the problem of national unity. The eloquent and moving words on this subject spoken by our Prime Minister at the opening of this debate will rank with the best in the history of our parliament. Fine speeches and mutual expressions of good will are most helpful, because they create an atmosphere and an environment without which true unity cannot be born. But we must not delude ourselves that having created a proper environment we can then leave the rest to royal commissions, provincial conferences and federal legislation. True unity cannot be manufactured; it must be created, and it is our job to create it.
The first step in creating national unity is to establish a solid foundation for it. In a democracy such as ours, which is based on the concept of man as a created being, there can be only one true basis of unity, and that is the acknowledgment of a divine Creator and obedience to His moral law. In fact, true democracy cannot function except within a framework of moral principles. We must realize too that real and lasting unity has a price tag on it, not in terms of dollars and cents but in terms of humility, of admitting where we have been wrong and endeavouring to put it right; in terms of caring for the other fellow, showing a willingness to consider other viewpoints and reconciling differences on a basis of what is right for the country as a whole. True unity cannot come from without. It cannot be brought about by outside agencies. It must come from within, and the price must be in terms of changed hearts, changed attitudes, changed outlooks and changed objectives. It cannot be done on the cheap.
True unity once established must be fostered and preserved. This requires a strong national purpose. A national purpose for the world in which we live today must be bigger than ourselves. It must be bigger even than our own country. It must be global in scope, something that we can give ourselves to completely, something we can lose ourselves in.

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that our national purpose should be nothing less than the creation of a completely new order of society in which the world's resources would be used for the benefit of all and for the exploitation of none. That gallant young soldier whose epitaph was quoted by our Prime Minister did not die just for Canada. He died for a better world for all mankind, for a new order of society where all people would live together in harmony, decency, dignity and peace; where everyone would care enough and would share enough so that everyone would have enough.
Our young people may never again be asked to die for their country, but they are being asked to live for their country and that may prove to be even more difficult. We deplore the recent display of "Beatlemania" and other similar phenomena so prevalent among our young people. Could not the reason be that we of our generation have never given them anything big enough to live for? We can correct that right now if we are prepared to honestly face our country as it is and determine to put right what is wrong in it.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should be less introspective and self centered and more concerned with problems of the world at large. Instead of looking inward, we should start looking outward at the 2J billion people who go to bed hungry every night and the millions who are enslaved in poverty and disease with no future, no life expectancy beyond 40. What better national purpose can we have here in Canada, where we enjoy so many blessings including material abundance, than to take the lead in creating a society where there would be a better life for all? Here is a purpose big enough to unite us all. Serious as are the problems that face us in Canada, if we view them against the background of world problems we will see them in better perspective and in more correct proportions. Moreover, by dedicating ourselves to doing something about this human poverty and degradation both in our own country and in the world at large, we shall find an unfailing source of real and lasting unity, not only for ourselves but for future generations.

Mr. Speaker, in adding my contribution to the address in reply to the speech from the throne I should like to take advantage of the traditional privilege of complimenting the mover and seconder of the address. I think I should point out that these new members in the house are witnessing a parliament that is somewhat unusual. The parliament in which we are now taking part has brought.

to life an old custom that is known as bundling. I am told by those who know more than I do about the custom that bundling started at one time in the highlands of Scotland when the nights were cool and damp and many of the people lived in one room homes. Because in the nature of things there was no opportunity for the young people of the household to engage in those very necessary activities of youth, it was arranged that while the older people sat around and looked into the fire-place, from which they obtained their warmth, the younger people were allowed to wrap a blanket around themselves and lie side by side in a bed along the wall. This custom of bundling came to the New England colonies and has become a part of the American vocabulary.
I wish to begin my remarks by saying that bundling is not dead in Canada. We have a new type of bundling being practised, and this is the bundling of politicians. Some of these politicians are not happy with the use of the word "bundling". One of them did not deny that bundling was going on, but one did disclaim this fact somewhat. I shall quote from the Medicine Hat News of January 11, 1964 where the headline says:
Olson says Socreds are bundling, but...
He says they are not bundling with the Liberal party, but just with the Liberal government.
