speechtext:
Last night in the house the Liberals voted for the retention of the regressive 11 per cent sales tax, but I think to see the significance of that vote last night we have to look at the wider picture. I want to go quickly back over the last 14 years, starting with the time of the Paley report to the president of the United States in 1952. Hon. members will recall that the Paley report pointed out to the government of that country that some strategic reserves of the United States were already or soon would be in short supply, and advocated that those in private enterprise in that country engaged in the work of developing and processing resources and energy should seek abroad for new reserves.
One area in which the report recommended they should seek these reserves was Canada, because we had a stable economic structure and were known to keep our word both in business and in international affairs. As a result of advice of this type and as a result of the great potential of Canadian resources, our country received in 1954, 1955 and 1956 a tremendous influx of capital to secure ownership and management control over large reserves of our resources. This brought to Canada in those years a foreign exchange problem.
There were two courses open for any Canadian government to follow. One course was a policy of restriction, and there were many advocates of such a policy. The idea was that we should put up barriers against capital and goods coming into our country, even to the extent of stopping $1 billion of United States goods from coming into Canada, and that we should add to this a policy of barring investment. It was suggested that we should impose heavier taxes as a part of this overall restrictive policy, which was referred to as pulling ourselves up by our own bootstraps or tightening our belts and getting out of the hole in 10 or 20 years.
That was one course which was supported by some, but there was another course. It was the course the former government took in facing this difficulty. That course was to bring before parliament an expanded trade program, to enter upon a program of expanded international credit sales; and from June of 1961 to start deliberately to bring our dollar into a realistic relationship with the currency
The Address-Mr. Hamilton of other countries on the basis of our real exchange situation. We also moved into an extended program of research. This was actually started in wholesale measure in the years 1958 and 1959. My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was one of the leaders in that effort.
I outlined this research program, I think, during the 1959 debate on the address in reply. We went further than that and earlier than that, in changing the oil and gas regulations and the mining regulations dealing with the areas we had under our control in the Northwest Territories and the lands beneath the sea. We did so in order to ensure that these great reservoirs of future wealth in the form of minerals and of energy would always be preserved for Canadians, not only in so far as the control of these resources was concerned but in the right to participate in their exploitation. These mining regulations, these oil and gas regulations, were a landmark in the attempt of Canadians to have more control over the economic future of their country. Now we see stories in the newspapers that section 45 is to be abandoned and the regulations changed.
I should like to point out one thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is throughout this attempt to get control of our resources and energy there was no question of a repudiation of contract. All contracts in effect before the date of these regulations were honoured, and I hope they are still being honoured. Any future oil, gas or mineral leases would be made under our regulations.
What happened when the new government took office? Everyone knows that through their budget they turned back from a policy of expansion, in trying to meet our balance of payments difficulties, to a policy of restriction. They turned to transfer taxes to bother the flow of capital. This transfer tax repudiated contracts. They turned to the 11 per cent sales tax, and they tried to take away with one fell swoop all the good we got out of the 7i per cent dollar devaluation.
I should like to mention, too, that when you voted last night you were voting to go along with the old policy that we said in 1957, 1959 and 1960 would lead to expansion, or to stay with the new policy of the new government, a policy of restriction which will eventually throttle the rising economy we have had since June, 1961.

speechtext:
I thank you for your guidance, Mr. Speaker. I just made a passing reference, and I do not believe I was too far out of order.
In the remaining time that is left to me I should like to deal swiftly with two items which I think have a bearing on the government's policy, not deliberate but blundering and unintentional, of restriction. I have asked some questions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dating back as far as May of last year concerning international commodity agreements. These questions can be found by looking at Hansard for May 31,
1963,	page 495; June 5, 1963, page 685; February 20, 1964, page 39; February 25,
1964,	page 201.
What do all these questions indicate? They indicate that there was a change of policy on the part of the government during the last year toward these international commodity agreements. If you look at the minister's answers in May and June of last year you will find he was in favour of long range international commodity agreements. The other day he gave an answer indicating that the time was not propitious for entering into these agreements.
I have all these statements before me, and what do they say? First of all, in order to build up my case, I ask what are the purposes of international commodity agreements? One purpose is to give international stability in the prices of primary products. However, there is another purpose which has come to the fore in the last 15 years, and that is to help those nations of the world to which the hon. member from Newfoundland was referring, which need help. These people can be helped by giveaways, but that hurts their pride. They would prefer to be helped on a solid basis of sound trading between the developing nations of the world and the other trading nations. Most of these nations have just one or two products to sell. If you think in terms of western wheat you have the complete parallel.
In 1949 we finally won our long battle in western Canada to get an international wheat agreement. Now every three years we negotiate a minimum price and a maximum price. The minimum price protects the producer and the maximum price protects the consumer. You try to pick a price that gives the producer a living without gouging the consumer. Here we have this example of protection for products outside our country; we have good protection for our wheat. Would the producers of sugar around this world not like that same stability?
We have had an international agreement on sugar. When the government changed, one of the first questions I asked of the Prime
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
Minister can be found in Hansard for May 31, 1963, page 495. It reads in part as follows;
I wonder whether I might ask the Prime Minister a question on the same subject but in a slightly different vein. Now that the United States Senate has ratified the international commodity agreement on coffee, will the Canadian government take the lead in pressing for completion of the international agreement on sugar?
The Minister of Trade and Commerce replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, it is the policy of this government to encourage international commodity arrangements-
Then he went on to describe how the government favours them. Then if you read Hansard for June 5, 1963, you will find the real reason for not renewing the sugar agreement, which would have protected consumers of the United States and Canada against this tremendous price increase we experienced during the last year. There was a disagreement over Cuba. In other words, because of Cuba's part in the negotiations it was found impossible to get all the countries into the agreement. Hon. members are allowed only one question as to which country was objecting to Cuba. We have had these high prices for sugar and all these questions in the house. Those people who depend upon sugar for a living still have not got their agreement renewed.
If you read the long answer by the minister you will find that there was agreement finally. Then he said if it were found that less than the required number of countries had become parties to this protocol by January 1, 1964, the governments that had signed, ratified, accepted or acceded to this protocol might agree to put it into force amongst themselves. Why did this government if it believed in giving some sort of fair deal not only to our own consumers but to the producers of these newly developing countries, not stand up and say they would enter into an agreement? Why did they stand up and say, "We do not think it is propitious to enter into an agreement"? They did so because they are thinking in the old fashioned way of squeezing down the poor, unhappy country that has no bargaining power and which is dependent upon one or two products. It is all part of the restrictive attitude of mind that unconsciously dominates this government.
I could go through agreement after agreement to illustrate my point. The government of which I was a member was proud to take the lead in the O.E.C.D. in talks with our United States friends and talks with the other countries of the world concerning long range agreements when we knew they were trying to give these poor-I almost said devils- trying to make a living on sugar a fair price.

The world price for sugar was slightly less than 3 cents a pound, and it rose to 14 cents or 15 cents a pound recently. If there had been a price of between 5 cents and 8 cents a pound established under an agreement we would have doubled the price to the producer and the price to the consumer would not have been too high. This government unwittingly stuck a dagger into the hearts of the newly developing nations that were looking to Canada to continue this leadership and give them some form of justice.
There are so many things I want to say, Mr. Speaker, but I must watch the clock and I have just three minutes left. In those three minutes I want to speak not of sugar but of all the other nations of the world seeking the light. For several years I have felt that one of the great underdeveloped markets for the western world has been the Orient and the countries behind the iron curtain.
I went to China in 1961 to ask if they were willing to continue the long range trade agreement beyond 1963. They said they were if they could find their way out of various technical and trade difficulties. Since Canada could not absorb all their goods they could never begin to pay bilaterally for the big wheat sales we made to them, so I have been trying to figure out ideas to help them. I invited the Chinese to send a trade delegation to this country in 1961, and another came here in 1962, at the time of the election when everything was in confusion. I think western civilization's long search for China as a market for the western world is over. Ever since the days of Marco Polo men have tried to contact Cathay. Many met a frozen death trying to find their way to China, but now I think we have found our way. So in my conversations with the Chinese I have suggested various things that would help solve their technical and trading difficulties whereby they would have better access to the markets of the world.
Just a few weeks ago I received a letter from the Chinese inviting me to visit their country in the month of March next. I shall be leaving about the middle of March to continue the discussions I had with them in April, 1961; only this time I hope to be dealing with officials in the capital city of their country, and I hope to be able to point out the many products we have in Canada. I hope to be able to add some ideas to their own thinking on how to get their products into the western markets, so that great country of 700 million people can be drawn more and more into the orbit of the trading nations of the world and, as we talk together and trade together, I hope in the long run this will lead to more and more friendliness and a greater chance for peace in the world.
The Address-Mr. Langlois [Translation]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Indeed, it was hard to praise such an empty speech, because in a case like that, one can easily find oneself blowing a lot of hot air. However, they performed their task creditably.

I should like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle concerning a little bit of last year's administration. He said that the Liberals supported a funny money policy in an effort to overthrow the Conservative government. It might be funny money to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, but for my own part I would just as soon start to support funny money as start to support funny people.
A few minutes ago he was criticizing the Liberal government, and he had reason to do that. There is no reason to congratulate it, and he was blaming the government for having no policy. But, Mr. Speaker, I hope he remembers that on a national television broadcast a couple of weeks ago the hon. member for Three Rivers, when asked a point blank question, "What is the difference between the Liberal and the Conservative party so far as policy is concerned?" answered, "There is no difference. Just the men make the difference "
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that is not much.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard several speeches in which the beautiful sentences and the noble sentiments in favour of national unity were not lacking.
There is at the present time some friction between this country's two great nations: the French Canadian nation on the one hand and the Anglo-Saxon nation on the other. Maybe we should go back to the beginning of our history to find the basic reason for that misunderstanding.
If we study the present situation in Canada -I mean the province of Quebec and the Anglo-Saxon Canada, that is the nine other provinces if we study closely the economic situation of those two parties, we might find the basic reason for the awakening of French Canadians and why they insist on getting more from the federal government.
And that might greatly facilitate the task of bringing those two great races back to a perfect understanding.
Mr. Speaker, let us consider the province of Quebec and its general economic situation. Let us first look carefully at the industrial

The Address-Mr. Langlois field. As a member from a mining area, I can state that in the case of the asbestos industry, covering a period of 90 years, not a single secondary industry is manufacturing asbestos products.
Statistics show that for the year 1961-1962 the province of Quebec exported $131 million worth of asbestos to the United States, where it was transformed into secondary products which brought $2 billion to the Americans.
Why have no steps been taken up to now to process ourselves our raw materials, such as asbestos? This is not the only case. There is also the oil industry, as well as others, which supply our American neighbours and even other countries, so that they are able to process our raw materials and resell them to us as finished products.
The province of Quebec has very few secondary industries compared to the province of Ontario, for instance. That may be why the economy of the province of Quebec has not developed as it should have.
The same applies in the field of labour, and this is due to the lack of secondary industries in our province. Therefore, it necessarily and logically follows that in a province with a population of almost six million, the rate of unemployment is high. Compared with the rest of Canada, in the province of Quebec alone 45 per cent of the labour force is unemployed.
The matter is serious enough and even shocking for the province to wake up at a certain time and say: there is something lacking which might provide jobs for our people.
Mr. Speaker, 45 per cent of the unemployed in Canada are localized in the same province. This is intolerable. The answer to the problem is not to mess things up, but rather to attempt as soon as possible, to find a positive solution and put matters straight.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us consider the agricultural industry. I have here an article published in La Presse of February 25, 1964, and which states that in 1963, the agricultural income was rising in Saskatchewan and Alberta, but decreasing in the province of Quebec.
This is not the first time I have dealt with Quebec agriculture in the house and, believe me, Mr. Speaker, this will not be the last either.
Farm income in the province of Quebec shows a decrease at present. I have here an article published in the February 15, 1964 issue of La Tribune under the following title:
There is a severe need for technicians in Megantic and Wolfe counties.
Out of a total of 2,028 farms, 1,565 have registered sales amounting to more than $1,200 this year.

Mr. Speaker, half the farms have registered sales of more than $1,200 while the average per farm amounts to $850 in the province of Quebec.
The county of Megantic is, at the present time, quoted at 77 per cent among profitearning farms in the province. What about farms quoted at less than 77 per cent?
At present, the county of Megantic has an average income of $850 per farm, while in western Canada, the income is almost $6,000 this year.
That is the present situation in the province of Quebec; and yet we live in the same country, we share the same cost of living and have the same expenses. Western problems are well known but those of Quebec are overlooked.
We may be right in requesting a larger slice of the federal tax. It is the reason why we are witnessing at this time misunderstanding between Anglo-Saxons and French Canadians.
The Quebec farmers are saturated with taxes. I happen to have before me a brief which was submitted by the U.C.C. in which farmers threaten the provincial government with refusal to pay their taxes on their properties if there is no change.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the agronomists of Megantic county give us the following argument: Your sales quota is 77 per cent; you are not too badly off. This simply means: you are dying from hunger but less rapidly than others.
We will not tolerate reports of that kind any more than eastern or western farmers would.
I see that my time is running out. We have just heard the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) make a speech which he concluded by proposing an amendment to family allowances. It seems to me that he should have been more consistent since the members of his party voted three times against a subamendment on the same subject. And to show that we, at least, are consistent, I propose, seconded by the hon. member for Dorchester:
That all the words after "18 years" he struck out and the following be substituted therefor: and have not proposed at the same time a general increase in family allowances according to the cost of living index.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying the farmer, the labour class, in brief, the consumer generally, is exploited not only in the province of Quebec but in the whole country. I have before me an article written by Mr. Lorenzo Pare, chief editor of L'Action Catholique, in which he declares:
The consumer is king.

It is good to read such a thing from time to time and to remember it.
The consumer is king in our modem economy. It is a flattered, besieged, wooed king, who is often deceived by the multitude of those who curry his favours. But it is a king without any real defence against all those courtiers, who find a thousand and one reasons to incite him to grant them favours, to take away from him the dollars he earned the hard way.
President Johnson, in the United States, has just acknowledged the often critical position in which the American consumer finds himself. And
The Address-Mr. Langlois the Canadian consumer's position is not different. For, as Mr. Johnson stated: "For a long time, the consumer had little to say and had little weight in the government. As a worker, a businessman, a farmer, a lawyer, or a doctor, the citizen has been well represented. But as a consumer he took a back seat."
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock? [Text}
At six o'clock the house adjourned, pursuant to standing order.
